Pathology-2.question: ১) What is the normal value of reticulocyte?
Pathology-2.exp:
Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells that still contain residual ribosomal RNA. They are released from the bone marrow into the peripheral blood and mature into erythrocytes within 1–2 days.

The normal reticulocyte count in adults is approximately 0.5–2% of circulating red blood cells. Therefore, among the given options, 0.2–2.0% is the best answer as it encompasses the accepted normal range.

An increased reticulocyte count indicates increased bone marrow erythropoietic activity, as seen in hemolytic anemia or after acute blood loss. A decreased count suggests reduced red cell production, such as in aplastic anemia or untreated iron, vitamin B₁₂, or folate deficiency.

Pathology-2.question: ২) Anisocytosis means variations in the ---of RBC.
Pathology-2.exp:
Anisocytosis refers to variation in the size of red blood cells (RBCs). It is commonly seen in various types of anemia, especially iron deficiency anemia, megaloblastic anemia, and following blood transfusion. Anisocytosis is reflected by an increased red cell distribution width (RDW) on a complete blood count.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Shape variation is called poikilocytosis.

  • Diameter is only one dimension of cell size; anisocytosis refers to variation in the overall size of RBCs.

  • Iron content is not described by the term anisocytosis.

Pathology-2.question: ৩) What is the normal value of MCH?
Pathology-2.exp:
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH) is the average amount of hemoglobin present in each red blood cell. It is expressed in picograms (pg). The normal MCH value in adults is approximately 27–32 pg.

The other options represent different hematological parameters:

  • 6.7–7.6 µm (not mm) is the normal diameter of an RBC.

  • 31–35 g/dL is the normal Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC).

  • 76–96 fL (commonly 80–100 fL) is the normal Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV).

Pathology-2.question: ৪) Fragmented red cells are called--?
Pathology-2.exp:
Schistocytes are fragmented red blood cells produced by mechanical destruction of RBCs as they pass through damaged blood vessels or fibrin strands. On a peripheral blood smear, they appear as irregularly shaped, helmet-shaped, or triangular red cell fragments. They are a hallmark of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and are seen in conditions such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), and prosthetic heart valve–associated hemolysis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Spherocytes are small, spherical RBCs lacking central pallor.

  • Elliptocytes are oval or elliptical RBCs.

  • Burr cells (echinocytes) have numerous short, evenly spaced projections and are not fragmented cells.

Pathology-2.question: ৫) Pappenheimer bodies are found in---?
Pathology-2.exp:
Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules (ferritin aggregates) within red blood cells. They appear as small, coarse, basophilic inclusions on a Wright–Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear and can be confirmed as iron by Prussian blue stain.

They are characteristically seen in sideroblastic anemia, where there is defective incorporation of iron into heme despite adequate or increased iron stores. They may also be seen after splenectomy, in myelodysplastic syndromes, and occasionally in other conditions associated with iron overload.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Megaloblastic anemia is characterized by macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

  • Leukemia is not characteristically associated with Pappenheimer bodies.

  • Hemolytic anemia may show features such as reticulocytosis and spherocytes (depending on the cause), but Pappenheimer bodies are not a typical finding.

Pathology-2.question: ৬) ESR is low in--?
Pathology-2.exp:
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is influenced by the ability of red blood cells to form rouleaux. In sickle cell anemia, the abnormal sickle-shaped RBCs do not form rouleaux effectively, resulting in a low ESR.

The other options are associated with an increased ESR because they are inflammatory or infectious conditions with elevated acute-phase proteins (especially fibrinogen), which promote rouleaux formation:

  • Acute rheumatic fever

  • Rheumatoid arthritis

  • Tuberculosis

Pathology-2.question: ৭) Which is not an absolute indication for bone marrow aspiration??
Pathology-2.exp:
Bone marrow aspiration is an essential investigation in disorders where direct evaluation of the bone marrow is required, such as:

  • Aplastic anemia – to demonstrate a hypocellular marrow.

  • Multiple myeloma – to identify clonal plasma cell infiltration.

  • Lymphoma – for assessment of bone marrow involvement and staging.

In immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), the diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by isolated thrombocytopenia after excluding other causes. Bone marrow aspiration is not routinely required and is performed only in selected situations, such as atypical clinical features, older patients, or before certain therapies.

Pathology-2.question: ৮) Bone deformities occur in which type of anemia?
Pathology-2.exp:
Thalassemia, particularly β-thalassemia major, is characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis, leading to marked bone marrow expansion. This expansion causes bone deformities, especially in the skull and facial bones, resulting in features such as frontal bossing, prominent malar bones, and maxillary overgrowth (chipmunk facies). Skull X-rays may show the characteristic "hair-on-end" appearance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Aplastic anemia causes bone marrow failure without marrow expansion or bone deformities.

  • Megaloblastic anemia causes ineffective erythropoiesis but does not produce characteristic bone deformities.

  • Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) does not cause bone deformities.

Pathology-2.question: ৯) Stem cell appear in yolk sac in---?
Pathology-2.exp:
The first hematopoietic stem cells appear in the blood islands of the yolk sac during the 3rd week of embryonic life. This is the earliest site of hematopoiesis in the embryo and primarily produces primitive nucleated erythrocytes.

As fetal development progresses, hematopoiesis shifts sequentially:

  • 3rd week: Yolk sac

  • 6th week onward: Liver (major hematopoietic organ during fetal life)

  • Later fetal life: Spleen

  • From about the 5th month onward: Bone marrow, which becomes the principal site after birth.

Pathology-2.question: ১০) Normal myeloid/ erythroid ratio is---?
Pathology-2.exp:
The myeloid-to-erythroid (M:E) ratio is the ratio of granulocytic (myeloid) precursors to erythroid precursors in the bone marrow. The normal M:E ratio is approximately 2:1 to 4:1, with 3:1 being the commonly accepted average and the best single answer.

The M:E ratio may change in disease:

  • It is increased in conditions with myeloid hyperplasia, such as infections and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

  • It is decreased in erythroid hyperplasia, as seen in hemolytic anemia and thalassemia.

Pathology-2.question: ১১) Nucleated red cells may be present in---?
Pathology-2.exp:
Nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) are immature erythroid cells that are normally confined to the bone marrow. Their presence in the peripheral blood indicates marked bone marrow stress or intense erythropoiesis.

In thalassemia major, severe ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic hemolysis stimulate marked bone marrow hyperplasia, leading to the premature release of nucleated red cells into the circulation. This is a characteristic peripheral blood smear finding.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) typically shows microcytic hypochromic RBCs but not nucleated red cells.

  • ITP is an isolated platelet disorder with normal red cell maturation.

  • Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder affecting platelet adhesion and does not cause nucleated red cells in the peripheral blood.

Pathology-2.question: ১২) Which is not a cardinal features of folate deficiency?
Pathology-2.option3: Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord
Pathology-2.exp:
Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with features such as glossitis, weakness, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Unlike vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, it does not produce neurological manifestations.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is a characteristic feature of vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, resulting from demyelination of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Patients develop impaired vibration and position sense, sensory ataxia, and spastic weakness.

Although peripheral neuropathy is also typically associated with vitamin B₁₂ deficiency rather than folate deficiency, subacute combined degeneration is the classic distinguishing neurological feature. Therefore, it is the best single answer.

Pathology-2.question: ১৩) Schilling test is done for the assessment of---?
Pathology-2.exp:
The Schilling test is used to assess vitamin B₁₂ absorption and to determine whether vitamin B₁₂ deficiency is due to intrinsic factor deficiency (pernicious anemia) or another cause of malabsorption.

In the classic test, the patient is given radiolabeled vitamin B₁₂ orally, followed by a large intramuscular dose of unlabeled vitamin B₁₂. Urinary excretion of the labeled vitamin is then measured. Low urinary excretion indicates impaired absorption. Repeating the test with intrinsic factor helps identify pernicious anemia if absorption normalizes.

The other options are incorrect because the Schilling test is not used to assess:

  • Iron

  • Folic acid

  • Pyridoxine (Vitamin B₆)

Pathology-2.question: ১৪) Which one is normal haemoglobin?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hb-F (fetal hemoglobin) is a normal physiological hemoglobin present during fetal life and in small amounts in healthy adults (usually <1%). It consists of two α and two γ chains (α₂γ₂) and has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin, facilitating oxygen transfer from the mother to the fetus.

The other options are abnormal hemoglobin variants:

  • Hb-S – associated with sickle cell disease.

  • Hb-C – associated with hemoglobin C disease.

  • Hb-E – a common abnormal hemoglobin variant, especially in Southeast Asia, associated with Hb E disease and Hb E/β-thalassemia.

Although Hb-A (α₂β₂) is the normal adult hemoglobin, it is not listed among the options. Therefore, the best answer is Hb-F.

Pathology-2.question: ১৫) Which is not a cause of pancytopenia?
Pathology-2.exp:
Pancytopenia is the reduction of all three blood cell lines: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. It results from decreased bone marrow production or increased peripheral destruction/sequestration.

The following are recognized causes of pancytopenia:

  • Aplastic anemia – causes bone marrow failure with reduction of all hematopoietic cell lines.

  • Radiotherapy – suppresses bone marrow, leading to pancytopenia.

  • Hypersplenism – causes excessive sequestration and destruction of blood cells, producing pancytopenia.

Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an increase in red cell mass, often accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis. Therefore, it is not a cause of pancytopenia. (Although advanced post-polycythemic myelofibrosis may eventually cause cytopenias, this is not the typical presentation.)

Pathology-2.question: ১৬) Estimation of red cell lifespan is done by use of radioactive --?
Pathology-2.exp:
The red cell lifespan is measured by labeling the patient's red blood cells with radioactive chromium-51 (^51Cr) and then monitoring the rate at which the labeled cells disappear from the circulation. This is the standard and classical method for assessing red cell survival and is particularly useful in the evaluation of hemolytic anemia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cobalt (Co) is mainly used in studies related to vitamin B₁₂ metabolism.

  • Carbon (C) isotopes are not used for red cell survival studies.

  • Iodine (I) isotopes are commonly used in thyroid investigations.

Pathology-2.question: ১৭) What is not the evidence of red cell damage?
Pathology-2.exp:
Howell-Jolly bodies are small, round nuclear DNA remnants within red blood cells. They are typically seen after splenectomy, in functional hyposplenism, or in severe megaloblastic anemia. They indicate impaired splenic function rather than red cell damage.

The other options are evidence of red cell damage:

  • Fragmented red cells (schistocytes) indicate mechanical destruction of RBCs, as seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

  • Heinz bodies are aggregates of denatured hemoglobin caused by oxidative damage to RBCs.

  • Spherocytes result from loss of red cell membrane, as seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Pathology-2.question: ১৮) What is not a cause of lymphocytic leukemoid blood picture?
Pathology-2.exp:
A lymphocytic leukemoid blood picture is characterized by a marked increase in lymphocytes, mimicking leukemia but occurring as a reactive process.

It is classically seen in:

  • Whooping cough (pertussis) – causes marked absolute lymphocytosis.

  • Infectious mononucleosis – characterized by lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.

Measles typically causes leukopenia with lymphopenia rather than lymphocytic leukocytosis. Therefore, it is not a cause of a lymphocytic leukemoid blood picture.

Meningitis may produce a leukemoid reaction, but it is usually neutrophilic (especially in bacterial meningitis), not lymphocytic. However, among the given options, measles is the best single answer because it is characteristically associated with lymphopenia.

Pathology-2.question: ১৯) Disorders producing paraproteinaemia excludes…?
Pathology-2.exp:
Paraproteinaemia refers to the presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) or its fragments in the blood, produced by a clone of plasma cells or B lymphocytes.

It is characteristically seen in:

  • Multiple myeloma – the commonest cause of paraproteinaemia.

  • Primary (AL) amyloidosis – due to deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains.

  • CLL – may be associated with monoclonal gammopathy in some patients because it is a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is not typically associated with paraproteinaemia. Although polyclonal immunoglobulin abnormalities may occur, the production of a monoclonal paraprotein is not a characteristic feature.

Pathology-2.question: ২০) What is the most common cause of leukoerythroblastic blood picture?
Pathology-2.option1: Secondary metastatic carcinoma in bone marrow
Pathology-2.exp:
A leukoerythroblastic blood picture is characterized by the presence of immature myeloid cells and nucleated red blood cells in the peripheral blood. It usually indicates bone marrow infiltration or severe marrow stress, causing immature cells to be released into the circulation.

The most common cause is secondary metastatic carcinoma involving the bone marrow (myelophthisic anemia). Common primary tumors include breast, prostate, and lung cancers.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Lymphoma can infiltrate the bone marrow and produce a leukoerythroblastic picture, but it is less common than metastatic carcinoma.

  • Multiple myeloma may involve the marrow but is a less frequent cause of a classic leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

  • Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases are infiltrative storage disorders that can occasionally produce this picture but are much less common.

Pathology-2.question: ২১) What is not true about non hodgkin’s lymphoma?
Pathology-2.option2: Single axial group of lymph node is usually involved
Pathology-2.exp:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) typically presents with multiple peripheral lymph nodes, non-contiguous spread, and frequent extranodal involvement (e.g., gastrointestinal tract, skin, CNS). Histologically, NHL usually shows a monomorphic proliferation of malignant lymphoid cells.

The statement "Single axial group of lymph node is usually involved" is characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma, not NHL. Hodgkin lymphoma usually begins in a single axial lymph node group (commonly cervical or mediastinal) and spreads in a contiguous manner.

The other options are true features of NHL:

  • Non-contiguous spread

  • Extranodal involvement is common

  • Monomorphic infiltration is usual

Pathology-2.question: ২২) What is the normal value of APTT?
Pathology-2.exp:
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) measures the integrity of the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways. It is used to evaluate deficiencies of factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen, and to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy.

The normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds (the exact reference range varies slightly among laboratories).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 10–14 seconds is the normal Prothrombin Time (PT).

  • 11–16 seconds is also within the typical range for PT, depending on the reagent used.

  • 6–10 minutes corresponds to the older whole blood clotting time, not APTT.

Pathology-2.question: ২৩) Hb electrophoresis is indicated in---?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is used to identify and quantify different types of hemoglobin. It is the investigation of choice for diagnosing thalassemia and other hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and Hb C disease.

In thalassemia, hemoglobin electrophoresis typically shows:

  • β-thalassemia trait: Increased HbA₂ (≥3.5%), with or without a mild increase in HbF.

  • β-thalassemia major: Markedly increased HbF with little or no HbA.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is diagnosed with iron studies (e.g., serum ferritin, serum iron, TIBC), not hemoglobin electrophoresis.

  • Anemia of chronic disease is evaluated by inflammatory markers and iron studies.

  • Sideroblastic anemia is diagnosed by bone marrow examination showing ring sideroblasts and iron studies.

Pathology-2.question: ২৪) In which condition anemia does not occur?
Pathology-2.exp:
Anemia of chronic disease is commonly associated with chronic inflammatory and infectious conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), tuberculosis (TB), and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). These disorders produce inflammatory cytokines that impair iron utilization and suppress erythropoiesis.

In contrast, COPD classically causes secondary polycythemia due to chronic hypoxemia stimulating increased erythropoietin production. Although anemia can occur in some patients with advanced COPD because of chronic inflammation or other comorbidities, it is not the classic hematological finding.

Pathology-2.question: ২৫) Which of the following disease is not transmitted via blood?
Pathology-2.exp:
Tuberculosis (TB) is primarily transmitted through airborne droplet nuclei released when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, speaks, or sings. It is not considered a blood-borne infection.

The other options can be transmitted through blood:

  • Hepatitis C – transmitted through infected blood, contaminated needles, and blood transfusions.

  • Malaria – although mainly transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito, it can also be transmitted through blood transfusion, organ transplantation, or contaminated needles.

  • AIDS (HIV infection) – transmitted through infected blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child.

Pathology-2.question: ২৬) Which is not a cause of DIC?
Pathology-2.exp:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a pathological process characterized by widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in microvascular thrombosis and consumption of platelets and coagulation factors.

Common causes of DIC include:

  • Amniotic fluid embolism – a classic obstetric cause.

  • Snake bite – particularly viper envenomation, which can activate coagulation and precipitate DIC.

  • Septicaemia – especially Gram-negative sepsis, one of the most common causes of DIC.

Hemoglobin less than 9 g/dL is a manifestation of anemia, not a cause of DIC. Although DIC may itself lead to anemia due to bleeding or microangiopathic hemolysis, a low hemoglobin level does not trigger DIC.

Pathology-2.question: ২৭) All of the following is true about myeloblast except......?
Pathology-2.exp:
A myeloblast is an immature precursor of the granulocytic series. Its typical morphological features include:

  • High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio

  • Fine (less dense) chromatin

  • 2–5 prominent nucleoli (commonly 3–4)

Auer rods are not a normal feature of all myeloblasts. They are needle-shaped azurophilic cytoplasmic inclusions that may be present in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), particularly certain subtypes. Therefore, the statement "Auer rod present" is not universally true for myeloblasts.

Pathology-2.question: ২৮) which of the following isn't included in classical Hodgkin's lymphoma?
Pathology-2.exp:
The classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) is divided into four histological subtypes according to the WHO classification:

  • Nodular sclerosis – the most common subtype.

  • Mixed cellularity

  • Lymphocyte-rich

  • Lymphocyte-depleted

Histiocytic sarcoma is not a subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma. It is a rare malignant neoplasm of mature histiocytes (macrophages) and is classified separately from both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

Pathology-2.question: ২৯) JAK2 mutation is a characteristic feature of...?
Pathology-2.exp:
The JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation, most commonly JAK2 V617F, is the characteristic molecular abnormality in polycythaemia vera (PV/PRV). It is present in more than 95% of patients and leads to constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, resulting in uncontrolled proliferation of hematopoietic cells, particularly erythroid precursors.

Although JAK2 mutations may also be found in essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis, they are most strongly associated with polycythaemia vera.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AML is commonly associated with mutations such as FLT3, NPM1, and CEBPA.

  • ITP is an autoimmune disorder without a characteristic JAK2 mutation.

  • ALL is associated with abnormalities such as t(12;21) and t(9;22) (Philadelphia chromosome), not JAK2.

Pathology-2.question: ৩০) Leukopenia occurs in.....?
Pathology-2.exp:
Leukopenia is a characteristic hematological finding in typhoid fever. It occurs due to bone marrow suppression by Salmonella Typhi and is often accompanied by relative lymphocytosis and eosinopenia. The presence of fever with leukopenia is a classic clue to the diagnosis of typhoid.

The other options are less characteristic:

  • Tuberculosis usually has a normal or mildly elevated white blood cell count; leukopenia is uncommon.

  • Brucellosis may occasionally cause leukopenia, but it is not the typical or classic finding.

  • Rickettsial diseases may show normal or reduced leukocyte counts depending on the stage and organism, but leukopenia is less characteristic than in typhoid.

Pathology-2.question: ৩১) Which of the haemoglobinopathies occur in Bangladesh?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hemoglobin E (HbE) is the most common hemoglobinopathy in Bangladesh and is highly prevalent throughout South and Southeast Asia. It results from a mutation in the β-globin gene and may occur as:

  • HbE trait (heterozygous) – usually asymptomatic.

  • HbE disease (homozygous) – causes mild hemolytic anemia.

  • HbE/β-thalassemia – a common and clinically important disorder in Bangladesh, with severity ranging from mild to transfusion-dependent anemia.

The other options are uncommon in Bangladesh:

  • HbS is predominantly seen in individuals of African, Middle Eastern, and some Indian tribal ancestry.

  • HbC is mainly found in West Africa.

  • HbD occurs in parts of North India and Pakistan but is much less common in Bangladesh.

Pathology-2.question: ৩২) Anemia can be termed as severe when Hb level falls below.... g/dl?
Pathology-2.exp:
Severe anemia refers to a markedly reduced hemoglobin concentration that significantly impairs oxygen delivery to tissues. In many standard pathology and hematology textbooks, hemoglobin below 6 g/dL is considered severe anemia and is associated with a high risk of tissue hypoxia, cardiac failure, and the need for urgent evaluation and treatment.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 13 g/dL is within the normal range for adult males.

  • 11 g/dL represents mild anemia in many clinical settings.

  • 9 g/dL is generally considered moderate anemia, not severe.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৩) What is the staining characteristic of platelet?
Pathology-2.exp:
On a Wright–Giemsa or Leishman-stained peripheral blood smear, platelets appear as small, anucleate, purplish-blue (lilac) cytoplasmic fragments. They contain purple (azurophilic) granules within a pale blue cytoplasm, giving them an overall purplish-blue appearance.

The other options are incorrect because platelets do not normally stain:

  • Yellowish

  • Greenish

  • Pinkish

Pathology-2.question: ৩৪) What is the final stage of maturation during erythropoiesis?
Pathology-2.exp:
The stages of erythropoiesis are:

  • Proerythroblast

  • Basophilic erythroblast

  • Polychromatic erythroblast

  • Orthochromatic erythroblast (normoblast)

  • Reticulocyte

  • Mature erythrocyte

Among the given options, the orthochromatic erythroblast is the final nucleated stage of erythroid maturation. At this stage, the nucleus becomes small and pyknotic and is subsequently extruded, producing a reticulocyte, which then matures into a red blood cell within 1–2 days.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৫) Megakaryoblast resembles....?
Pathology-2.exp:
A megakaryoblast is the earliest recognizable precursor of the megakaryocytic lineage. Morphologically, it closely resembles a lymphoblast because both cells have:

  • A high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio

  • Scant, deeply basophilic cytoplasm

  • A round or oval nucleus with fine chromatin and prominent nucleoli

As the megakaryoblast matures, it undergoes endomitosis, resulting in a large, multilobed megakaryocyte that produces platelets.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Erythroblasts have progressively hemoglobinized cytoplasm.

  • Myeloblasts may contain azurophilic granules and, in leukemia, Auer rods.

  • Monoblasts are larger, with more abundant cytoplasm and often show nuclear folding.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৬) which anticoagulant is not used in blood transfusion?
Pathology-2.exp:
EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is not used for blood transfusion because it is unsuitable for storing donor blood. It strongly chelates calcium and may adversely affect red blood cell viability during storage. EDTA is primarily used as an anticoagulant for complete blood count (CBC) and peripheral blood smear examinations.

The anticoagulants used for blood collection and storage for transfusion include:

  • ACD (Acid Citrate Dextrose)

  • CPD (Citrate Phosphate Dextrose)

  • Disodium (or sodium) citrate, which was used historically and remains the basis of modern blood-preservation solutions.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৭) Which of the following is automated method for hemoglobin estimation?
Pathology-2.exp:
Modern automated hematology analyzers (cell counters) estimate hemoglobin as part of the complete blood count (CBC). After lysing the red blood cells, the analyzer measures hemoglobin photometrically using an automated method (many analyzers use cyanmethemoglobin or sodium lauryl sulfate-based methods internally).

The other options are manual laboratory methods:

  • Acid hematin (Sahli's) method – an older manual method with lower accuracy.

  • Oxyhemoglobin method – a manual spectrophotometric method, now rarely used.

  • Cyanmethemoglobin method – the classical reference manual method for hemoglobin estimation, but it is not the automated method referred to in this question.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৮) What may not be a cause of Dry tap?
Pathology-2.exp:
A dry tap refers to the failure to obtain bone marrow aspirate despite correct needle placement. It usually occurs when the marrow is fibrotic, markedly hypocellular, or densely infiltrated.

Common causes include:

  • Faulty technique – the needle may not be correctly positioned within the marrow cavity.

  • Aplastic anemia – severe hypocellularity may result in failure to aspirate marrow.

  • Myelosclerosis (myelofibrosis) – a classic cause of dry tap due to extensive marrow fibrosis.

Megaloblastic anemia typically produces a hypercellular bone marrow with marked erythroid hyperplasia. Bone marrow aspiration is usually easy to perform and yields abundant material. Therefore, it is not a cause of a dry tap.

Pathology-2.question: ৩৯) which of the following test doesn't correspond to diagnosis of hemophilia?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hemophilia A and B are deficiencies of factor VIII and factor IX, respectively. These factors belong to the intrinsic coagulation pathway, so the Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is prolonged.

The typical laboratory findings in hemophilia are:

  • Bleeding time (BT): Normal – platelet function is normal.

  • Clotting time (CT): Prolonged – due to defective coagulation.

  • APTT: Prolonged – the most characteristic laboratory abnormality.

  • Prothrombin time (PT): Normal – the extrinsic pathway is unaffected.

Pathology-2.question: ৪০) Leukemia is associated with which of the following genetic disease?
Pathology-2.exp:
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is strongly associated with an increased risk of leukemia, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), especially acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7) in children. Individuals with Down syndrome have a markedly higher risk of developing leukemia than the general population.

The other chromosomal disorders are not characteristically associated with leukemia:

  • Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18) – associated with multiple congenital anomalies but not leukemia.

  • Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) – associated with severe congenital malformations.

  • Turner syndrome (45,X) – associated with gonadal dysgenesis and congenital cardiovascular anomalies, not an increased risk of leukemia.

Pathology-2.question: ৪১) INR is used to assess the therapeutic effect of--?
Pathology-2.exp:
The International Normalized Ratio (INR) is a standardized form of the Prothrombin Time (PT) and is used to monitor the anticoagulant effect of coumarin derivatives, such as warfarin. Warfarin inhibits the synthesis of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, resulting in prolongation of the PT/INR.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Low molecular weight (LMW) heparin is usually monitored with anti-factor Xa activity when monitoring is required; INR is not useful.

  • High molecular weight (unfractionated) heparin is monitored using APTT, not INR.

  • Streptokinase is a thrombolytic agent, and its therapeutic effect is not monitored by INR.

Pathology-2.question: ৪২) Causes of non thrombocytopenic purpura does not includes which of the following?
Pathology-2.exp:
Non-thrombocytopenic purpura refers to purpura that occurs despite a normal platelet count. It is usually caused by vascular abnormalities, increased capillary fragility, or abnormal plasma proteins rather than a deficiency of platelets.

Examples include:

  • Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) – an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis with a normal platelet count.

  • Senile purpura – due to age-related loss of connective tissue support around blood vessels.

  • Paraproteinemia – abnormal plasma proteins can impair vascular integrity and platelet function without causing thrombocytopenia.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is characterized by immune-mediated destruction of platelets, resulting in thrombocytopenia. Therefore, it is a thrombocytopenic purpura, not a non-thrombocytopenic purpura.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৩) Factors of Hb synthesis excludes--?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hemoglobin synthesis requires several essential nutrients and cofactors. Among them:

  • Iron (Fe) is the central component of the heme molecule and is indispensable for hemoglobin formation.

  • Copper (Cu) plays an important role in iron metabolism, facilitating iron absorption and mobilization for hemoglobin synthesis.

  • Calcium (Ca) is not directly involved in heme synthesis, but it is a normal physiological mineral and has roles in many cellular processes.

Clavulanic acid is a β-lactamase inhibitor used in combination with antibiotics such as amoxicillin. It has no role in hemoglobin synthesis.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৪) Haematocrit doesn’t increases in which of the following?
Pathology-2.exp:
Hematocrit (packed cell volume, PCV) is the percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.

Hematocrit increases in conditions associated with increased red cell mass or reduced plasma volume, such as:

  • Congenital cyanotic heart disease – chronic hypoxia causes secondary polycythemia.

  • High altitude – hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production, increasing red cell mass.

In pregnancy, although red cell mass increases, plasma volume increases even more (about 40–50%), leading to physiological hemodilution. As a result, the hematocrit decreases, producing the so-called physiological anemia of pregnancy.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৫) Which one is the most common form of anemia in infancy & childhood?
Pathology-2.exp:
Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia in infancy and childhood worldwide. It commonly occurs between 6 months and 2 years of age due to:

  • Increased iron requirements during rapid growth.

  • Inadequate dietary iron intake (e.g., prolonged exclusive milk feeding).

  • Prematurity or low birth weight.

  • Chronic blood loss (less common).

The other options are much less common:

  • Hemolytic anemia – occurs in specific inherited or acquired disorders.

  • Megaloblastic anemia – usually due to folate or vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and is relatively uncommon.

  • Sideroblastic anemia – a rare disorder of heme synthesis.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৬) What is the desired change in CBC in Asthma?
Pathology-2.exp:
Bronchial asthma, particularly allergic (atopic) asthma, is characterized by eosinophilic inflammation of the airways. Therefore, the typical CBC finding is peripheral eosinophilia, which reflects the underlying IgE-mediated hypersensitivity response.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Monocytosis is more commonly seen in chronic infections and inflammatory disorders.

  • Neutrophilia is usually associated with bacterial infections, stress, or corticosteroid therapy rather than uncomplicated asthma.

  • Lymphopenia is not a characteristic finding in asthma.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৭) secondary polycythemia does not occur in..?
Pathology-2.exp:
Secondary polycythemia is an absolute increase in red cell mass caused by increased erythropoietin (EPO) production in response to hypoxia or ectopic EPO secretion.

It occurs in:

  • Emphysema – chronic hypoxemia stimulates EPO production.

  • Hydronephrosis – renal hypoxia may increase EPO secretion.

  • Cirrhosis of the liver may rarely be associated with secondary polycythemia, particularly when accompanied by hepatocellular carcinoma or other EPO-producing hepatic lesions.

Dehydration does not cause secondary polycythemia. Instead, it causes relative (spurious) polycythemia, in which the hematocrit is increased due to reduced plasma volume, while the red cell mass remains normal.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৮) Which is not a features of myeloblastic leukemia ?
Pathology-2.exp:
Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) is characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of myeloblasts in the bone marrow, leading to bone marrow failure.

Typical features of AML include:

  • Gum bleeding – due to thrombocytopenia (gingival infiltration may also occur, especially in monocytic variants).

  • Adult onset – AML is the most common acute leukemia in adults.

  • Thrombocytopenia – resulting in bleeding manifestations such as petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding.

Meningeal (CNS) involvement is much more characteristic of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), particularly in children. It is uncommon in AML and therefore is not a typical feature of myeloblastic leukemia.

Pathology-2.question: ৪৯) 49. von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a protein synthesised by...?
Pathology-2.exp:
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is synthesized by both:

  • Endothelial cells – the major source of plasma vWF. It is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies and released into the circulation.

  • Megakaryocytes – vWF is incorporated into the α-granules of platelets and is released during platelet activation.

vWF has two major functions:

  • Mediates platelet adhesion to damaged vascular endothelium by binding platelet GpIb receptors.

  • Acts as the carrier protein for factor VIII, protecting it from degradation.

Pathology-2.question: ৫০) 50. Which one is not non-immune hemolytic anemia?
Pathology-2.exp:
Non-immune hemolytic anemia results from red cell destruction without antibody-mediated mechanisms. Examples include:

  • Cardiac (prosthetic valve) hemolytic anemia – mechanical destruction of RBCs.

  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) – fragmentation of RBCs in conditions such as DIC, TTP, HUS, and severe hypertension.

  • Eclampsia/HELLP syndrome – may cause MAHA due to endothelial injury and microvascular fibrin deposition.

Hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) is an immune hemolytic anemia, caused by maternal IgG antibodies (most commonly anti-D in Rh incompatibility or ABO incompatibility) crossing the placenta and destroying fetal red blood cells.
